meta.title: Polish B2
meta.subtitle: 1,200 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Polish → English (see the Polish, recall the meaning) and English → Polish (see an English meaning, recall the Polish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1,200 words for level B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Poland's State Commission for the Certification of Proficiency in Polish as a Foreign Language examines at all six levels, but no official word list was found for any of them. So 1,067 of the 1,200 words were written for Folio, a topic at a time, for the topics the B2 exam is described as covering — sport and its fans, reading and reviews, driving, accidents, crime and witnesses, complaints, warnings and protests, the telephone, discussion and argument, interviews and formal writing, spelling and language, and the B1 topics taken further (work, housing, the media, law, health, relationships, nature, the arts and travel) — together with the adjectives of countries, adjectives made from nouns (lekarski from lekarz), abstract nouns made from adjectives (dojrzałość from dojrzały), diminutives, żaden, każdy and wszyscy, and the connectives of a formal text. They are Folio's choice, not the Commission's, and this is not an official word list. No word taught in the levels below is repeated. The other 133 are the commonest words of everyday Polish not already chosen, from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles, each word counted over all its forms. The cards are ordered by that frequency, so the words met most often come first; the 24 set phrases, which a list of single words cannot count, come last. Polish changes the endings of its nouns, adjectives and verbs, and many stems change with them, so each card carries the forms that cannot be guessed, read from a dictionary rather than generated. 603 nouns show their gender, three cases of the singular and two of the plural. 292 verbs show their aspect and its partner, the forms for ja (I), on (he) and oni (they) and the past of on — a perfective verb's being its future, since it has no present. 48 adjectives show their comparative and superlative. Real example sentences come with 917 of the 1,200 words, three apiece for 621, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Meanings, forms and parts of speech: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency ordering: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
